title: Action–reaction pairs and system momentum
prereq: PH02 Newton's third law; P01 signed momentum; P03 choosing the system.
goals: Locate third-law force pairs on distinct bodies.
Sum internal impulses only at the complete-system level.
Explain why externally driven pairs need not conserve their own momentum.

sections.heading: Third-law partners are different bodies
sections.body: Newton's third law pairs the force A exerts on B with the force B exerts on A over the same interval. These forces are equal and opposite, but they act on different bodies. They cannot cancel in the net force equation for A alone or B alone. Draw separate free-body diagrams.

sections.heading: Internal impulse sums to zero for the pair
sections.body: If both A and B belong to your chosen two-body system, their paired internal impulses cancel when you add their momentum changes. For an isolated pair, Δp_A + Δp_B = 0. That does not mean either individual's momentum is fixed.

sections.heading: Equal impulse is not equal speed
sections.body: Each body's change is Δv = J/m when its mass is constant. A smaller mass has a larger magnitude velocity change under an equal impulse. The total momentum can still sum to zero while the bodies travel in opposite directions.

sections.heading: Changing system boundaries changes the ledger
sections.body: An outside wall, device, ground or rope can deliver external impulse to the chosen pair. Then ΔP_system = J_external rather than zero. Even knowing total external impulse usually does not tell you how it was split between the two bodies.

worked.name: Foundation · unequal skaters
worked.setup: Resting A is 3 kg and B is 1 kg; A gains +6 N·s of impulse from B.
steps: Third law gives B a −6 N·s impulse.
A ends with v_A = +6/3 = +2 m/s; B with v_B = −6/1 = −6 m/s.
worked.check: The pair is isolated but each skater's momentum changed.

worked.name: Connected · outside impulse
worked.setup: A 4 kg and B 2 kg pair exchange −4/+4 N·s internally while an outside actuator gives the pair +3 N·s.
steps: Internal −4 and +4 cancel on the whole-pair ledger.
Without knowing where the external impulse was applied, individual velocities cannot be uniquely reconstructed.
worked.check: A single total equation cannot determine two individual unknowns.

worked.name: Transfer · push a wall
worked.setup: A skater pushes a wall and recoils backward.
steps: The wall's force on the skater is external to the skater-only system.
Its paired force is on the wall/Earth, not on the skater.
The skater-only momentum is therefore not required to stay constant.
worked.check: Third-law action–reaction always holds; isolation is a separate condition.

trap.wrong: Draw both third-law forces on one body so they cancel each other.
trap.repair: Draw each body's separate forces, then combine only after specifying the entire pair's boundary.

assumptions: Third-law impulses refer to the same contact interval and different bodies.
Negligible horizontal external impulse is required for pair momentum conservation.
When only total external impulse is known, separate final velocities may be underdetermined.

model.label: Teaching model: impulse on B (2 kg A / 4 kg B)

prompt.stem: Two skaters A (2 kg) and B (3 kg) start at rest on smooth ice. During a push A receives −6 N·s from B, and B receives +6 N·s from A. No appreciable external horizontal impulse acts. Determine each final signed velocity and the final combined momentum.
prompt.prediction: Will their speeds be equal? Will their total momentum still be zero?
prompt.boundaryPrompt: An outside mechanism adds NET +3 N·s to the TWO-SKATER SYSTEM during the same interval, but its distribution between A and B is not known. Find total final momentum. Can each final velocity be determined uniquely?

boundaryFields.label: Are individual final velocities uniquely determined?
